claim: Differential activation in individual columns of the periaqueductal grey (PAG) was observed during breathlessness and its conditioned anticipation.
source: Previously we observed differential activation in individual columns of the periaqueductal grey (PAG) during breathlessness and its conditioned anticipation (Faull et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Faull et al., 2016b).

claim: Activation was observed in ventrolateral PAG (vlPAG) and lateral PAG (lPAG), where activity scaled with breathlessness intensity ratings.
source: Activation was observed in ventrolateral PAG (vlPAG) and lateral PAG (lPAG), where activity scaled with breathlessness intensity ratings, revealing a potential interface between sensation and cognition during breathlessness.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lPAG was functionally correlated with cortical sensorimotor areas at rest.
source: At rest the lPAG was functionally correlated with cortical sensorimotor areas, conducive to facilitating fight/flight responses, and demonstrated increased synchronicity with the amygdala during breathlessness.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by resting state functional connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lPAG demonstrated increased synchronicity with the amygdala during breathlessness.
source: At rest the lPAG was functionally correlated with cortical sensorimotor areas, conducive to facilitating fight/flight responses, and demonstrated increased synchronicity with the amygdala during breathlessness.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by task functional connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vlPAG showed fronto-limbic correlations at rest.
source: The vlPAG showed fronto-limbic correlations at rest, whereas during breathlessness anticipation, reduced functional synchronicity was seen to both lPAG and motor structures, conducive to freezing behaviours.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by resting state functional connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During breathlessness anticipation, the vlPAG showed reduced functional synchronicity to both lPAG and motor structures.
source: The vlPAG showed fronto-limbic correlations at rest, whereas during breathlessness anticipation, reduced functional synchronicity was seen to both lPAG and motor structures, conducive to freezing behaviours.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by task functional connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Subjective perceptions of breathlessness are not simply a neurological reflection of lung function.
source: Subjective perceptions of breathlessness are not simply a neurological reflection of lung function (Banzett et al., 2000; Teeter and Bleecker, 1998), and can cause crippling anxiety when perceived as a direct threat to survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Banzett et al., 2000; Teeter and Bleecker, 1998).

claim: Breathlessness can cause crippling anxiety when perceived as a direct threat to survival.
source: Subjective perceptions of breathlessness are not simply a neurological reflection of lung function (Banzett et al., 2000; Teeter and Bleecker, 1998), and can cause crippling anxiety when perceived as a direct threat to survival.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the psychological impact of breathlessness.

claim: Perceptions of breathlessness rely on an intricate system of sensory and affective components within the brain.
source: These perceptions rely on an intricate system of sensory and affective components within the brain (Hayen et al., 2013b; Herigstad et al., 2011; Lansing et al., 2009), both perceiving ventilatory afferents and evaluating the threat value of these sensations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hayen et al., 2013b; Herigstad et al., 2011; Lansing et al., 2009).

claim: Repeated episodes of breathlessness can lead to conditioned associations between a stimulus and breathlessness.
source: Furthermore, repeated episodes of breathlessness can lead to conditioned associations between a stimulus (such as a flight of stairs) and breathlessness (De Peuter et al., 2004), inducing anticipatory threat behaviours such as freezing or activity avoidance (Hayen et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (De Peuter et al., 2004).

claim: Conditioned associations between a stimulus and breathlessness can induce anticipatory threat behaviours such as freezing or activity avoidance.
source: Furthermore, repeated episodes of breathlessness can lead to conditioned associations between a stimulus (such as a flight of stairs) and breathlessness (De Peuter et al., 2004), inducing anticipatory threat behaviours such as freezing or activity avoidance (Hayen et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Hayen et al., 2013b).

claim: The midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) is a key neural component in the behavioural modulation of breathing.
source: The midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) is a key neural component in both the behavioural modulation of breathing (Subramanian, 2013; Subramanian et al., 2008) and coordination of threat responses (Bandler et al., 2000; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Keay and Bandler, 2001; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Subramanian, 2013; Subramanian et al., 2008).

claim: The midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) is a key neural component in the coordination of threat responses.
source: The midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) is a key neural component in both the behavioural modulation of breathing (Subramanian, 2013; Subramanian et al., 2008) and coordination of threat responses (Bandler et al., 2000; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Keay and Bandler, 2001; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bandler et al., 2000; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Keay and Bandler, 2001; Tovote et al., 2016).

claim: The PAG is divided into four longitudinal columns on each side.
source: The PAG is divided into four longitudinal columns (ventrolateral, vlPAG; lateral, lPAG; dorsolateral, dlPAG; dorsomedial, dmPAG) on each side, and is postulated to act as an interface for behavioural control (Bandler et al., 2000; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Benarroch, 2012; Keay and Bandler, 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The PAG is postulated to act as an interface for behavioural control.
source: The PAG is divided into four longitudinal columns (ventrolateral, vlPAG; lateral, lPAG; dorsolateral, dlPAG; dorsomedial, dmPAG) on each side, and is postulated to act as an interface for behavioural control (Bandler et al., 2000; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Benarroch, 2012; Keay and Bandler, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bandler et al., 2000; Bandler and Shipley, 1994; Benarroch, 2012; Keay and Bandler, 2001).

claim: The PAG has been implicated in many basic survival functions including cardiovascular, motor and pain responses.
source: The PAG has previously been implicated in many basic survival functions including cardiovascular, motor and pain responses such as vocalization or blood pressure regulation (De Oca et al., 1998; Mobbs et al., 2007; Paterson, 2014; Pereira et al., 2010; Tracey et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (De Oca et al., 1998; Mobbs et al., 2007; Paterson, 2014; Pereira et al., 2010; Tracey et al., 2002).

claim: The lPAG and dlPAG are thought to orchestrate 'active' responses when a threat is perceived as escapable.
source: An integrative theory of these behaviours postulates that the lPAG and dlPAG are thought to orchestrate 'active' responses (such as fight or flight responses) when a threat is perceived as escapable (Bandler and Carrive, 1988; Carrive, 1993; Depaulis et al., 1992; Keay and Bandler, 2001; Yardley and Hilton, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Bandler and Carrive, 1988; Carrive, 1993; Depaulis et al., 1992; Keay and Bandler, 2001; Yardley and Hilton, 1986).

claim: The vlPAG is thought to be involved with 'freezing' type behaviours from inescapable threats.
source: Conversely, the vlPAG is thought to be involved with 'freezing' type behaviours from inescapable threats (Carrive and Bandler, 1991; Keay et al., 1997; Lovick, 1993; Tovote et al., 2016), including conditioned anticipation of breathlessness in humans (Faull et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Carrive and Bandler, 1991; Keay et al., 1997; Lovick, 1993; Tovote et al., 2016).

claim: The vlPAG is involved in conditioned anticipation of breathlessness in humans.
source: Conversely, the vlPAG is thought to be involved with 'freezing' type behaviours from inescapable threats (Carrive and Bandler, 1991; Keay et al., 1997; Lovick, 1993; Tovote et al., 2016), including conditioned anticipation of breathlessness in humans (Faull et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Faull et al., 2016b).

claim: Tovote and colleagues mapped direct neuronal connections from the central nucleus of the amygdala to the vlPAG, and onwards to premotor areas in the ponto-medullary reticular formation to underlie freezing behaviours.
source: In recent work to understand this circuitry in animals, Tovote and collegues (Tovote et al., 2016) intricately mapped direct neuronal connections from the central nucleus of the amygdala to the vlPAG, and onwards to premotor areas in the ponto-medullary reticular formation to underlie freezing behaviours.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Tovote et al., 2016).

claim: Activity can be localised to the lPAG during breath holds.
source: This work revealed that activity can be localised to the lPAG during breath holds (Faull et al., 2015), to the vlPAG during conditioned anticipation of breathlessness, and to the lPAG during breathlessness itself (Faull et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Faull et al., 2015).

claim: Activity can be localised to the vlPAG during conditioned anticipation of breathlessness.
source: This work revealed that activity can be localised to the lPAG during breath holds (Faull et al., 2015), to the vlPAG during conditioned anticipation of breathlessness, and to the lPAG during breathlessness itself (Faull et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Faull et al., 2016b).

claim: Activity can be localised to the lPAG during breathlessness itself.
source: This work revealed that activity can be localised to the lPAG during breath holds (Faull et al., 2015), to the vlPAG during conditioned anticipation of breathlessness, and to the lPAG during breathlessness itself (Faull et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Faull et al., 2016b).

claim: Functional connectivity within neuroimaging is a measure of the temporal synchronicity of activity within structures across the brain.
source: 'Functional connectivity' within neuroimaging is a measure of the temporal synchronicity of activity within structures across the brain, and is thought to be related to the temporal coherence of neuronal activity in anatomically distinct regions (Gerstein and Perkel, 1969; van den Heuvel et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gerstein and Perkel, 1969; van den Heuvel et al., 2010).

claim: Forty healthy, right-handed individuals were trained using an aversive delay-conditioning paradigm to associate simple shapes with either a breathlessness stimulus or no loading.
source: Forty healthy, right-handed individuals were trained using an aversive delay-conditioning paradigm to associate simple shapes with either a breathlessness stimulus in the form of inspiratory resistive loading (100% contingency pairing) or no loading (0% contingency pairing).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and subject population.

claim: Mean intensity scores were significantly greater for breathlessness compared to unloaded breathing conditions (46.5% vs. 2.8%, p<0.001).
source: Mean intensity and anxiety scores were significantly greater for breathlessness compared to unloaded breathing conditions using a paired, two-tailed t-test (intensity (±SD): 46.5 (16.0)% vs. 2.8 (3.5)%, p<0.001; anxiety: (±SD) 34.0 (18.8)% vs. 2.5 (3.9)%, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Mean anxiety scores were significantly greater for breathlessness compared to unloaded breathing conditions (34.0% vs. 2.5%, p<0.001).
source: Mean intensity and anxiety scores were significantly greater for breathlessness compared to unloaded breathing conditions using a paired, two-tailed t-test (intensity (±SD): 46.5 (16.0)% vs. 2.8 (3.5)%, p<0.001; anxiety: (±SD) 34.0 (18.8)% vs. 2.5 (3.9)%, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Significantly increased mean BOLD activity was seen in the vlPAG (right) during anticipation of breathlessness.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Faull et al., 2016b), significantly increased mean BOLD activity was seen in the vlPAG (right) during anticipation of breathlessness, with an additional small cluster seen in the lPAG (left) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data and references Figure 1.

claim: An additional small cluster of BOLD activity was seen in the lPAG (left) during anticipation of breathlessness.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Faull et al., 2016b), significantly increased mean BOLD activity was seen in the vlPAG (right) during anticipation of breathlessness, with an additional small cluster seen in the lPAG (left) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data and references Figure 1.

claim: No mean BOLD activity was observed in the PAG when averaged across the group during breathlessness.
source: While no mean BOLD activity was observed in the PAG when averaged across the group during breathlessness, a significant correlation was found between lPAG and subjective scores of breathlessness intensity (Figure 2), consistent with the location of the lPAG activity observed during anticipation.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: A significant correlation was found between lPAG activity and subjective scores of breathlessness intensity.
source: While no mean BOLD activity was observed in the PAG when averaged across the group during breathlessness, a significant correlation was found between lPAG and subjective scores of breathlessness intensity (Figure 2), consistent with the location of the lPAG activity observed during anticipation.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data and references Figure 2.

claim: No PAG activity was found to scale with anxiety during either anticipation or breathlessness.
source: No PAG activity was found to scale with anxiety during either anticipation or breathlessness.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: During anticipation of breathlessness, significantly increased BOLD activity was seen in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, supplementary motor cortex, middle and posterior cingulate cingulate cortices, anterior and middle insula, subthalamic nucleus, operculum, cerebellar I-IV, primary visual cortex and primary sensory cortex.
source: Significantly increased BOLD activity was seen in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, supplementary motor cortex, middle and posterior cingulate cingulate cortices, anterior and middle insula, subthalamic nucleus, operculum, cerebellar I-IV, primary visual cortex and primary sensory cortex.

claim: During breathlessness, significantly increased BOLD activity was seen in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, putamen, caudate nucleus, primary sensory and motor cortices, supplementary motor cortex, middle cingulate cortex, anterior and middle insula, subthalamic nucleus, operculum, cerebellar I-IV, primary visual cortex and primary sensory cortex.

claim: During breathlessness, decreased BOLD activity was seen in the anterior and posterior cingulate cortices, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, inferior precuneus, hippocampus and amygdala, primary sensory cortex, and pontine nuclei.
source: Decreased BOLD activity was seen in the anterior and posterior cingulate cortices, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, inferior precuneus, hippocampus and amygdala, primary sensory cortex, and pontine nuclei (Figure 1).

source: The vlPAG seed showed significant functional connectivity to the right dorsomedial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, anterior/middle insula and amygdala, and bilateral connectivity to the ventral posterolateral, ventrolateral and dorsomedial nuclei of the thalamus, primary visual cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, hippocampus and parahippocampal gyri, subthalamic nucleus and I-IV, V, VI, crus-I lobes of the cerebellum (Figure 3).

claim: During breathlessness, the intra-PAG connectivity of the lPAG to the dlPAG and dmPAG inversely scaled with breathlessness intensity scores.

claim: The resting connectivity profile of the lPAG aligns with current theories of threat-induced behaviors where the lPAG is functionally connected to sensorimotor structures in preparation for fight/flight.
source: We have revealed resting functional connectivity profiles of these active PAG columns with the wider cortex that align with current theories of threat-induced behaviors, where the lPAG is functionally connected to sensorimotor structures in preparation for fight/flight, whilst the vlPAG is functionally connected to affective and evaluative prefrontal areas.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the resting connectivity data and comparison to existing theories.

claim: The resting connectivity profile of the vlPAG aligns with current theories of threat-induced behaviors where the vlPAG is functionally connected to affective and evaluative prefrontal areas.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the resting connectivity data and comparison to existing theories.

source: Furthermore, during anticipation of breathlessness, the vlPAG demonstrated reduced connectivity to both the lPAG and sensorimotor structures, consistent with a potential 'freeze' response.

source: This profile demonstrates plausible pathways for involvement in active responses through functional sensorimotor connections to the primary motor and sensory cortices and caudate nucleus (Cools, 1980).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the connectivity data and supported by a citation (Cools, 1980).

source: The lPAG showed no changes in connectivity profile during anticipation, while during breathlessness exhibited increased connectivity to the amygdala correlating with subjective anxiety scores.

claim: The lPAG showed no changes in connectivity profile during anticipation.

claim: The increased connectivity between lPAG and amygdala during breathlessness reveals a potential anxiety-encoding pathway.
source: These results reveal a potential anxiety-encoding pathway through the amygdala during the perception of the breathlessness stimulus (Davis, 1992; Stein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the connectivity data and supported by citations (Davis, 1992; Stein et al., 2007).

claim: The conditioned anticipation of a resistive load represents an inescapable respiratory threat.
source: In the current study, the conditioned anticipation of a resistive load represents an inescapable respiratory threat; a human threat analogue to experiments demonstrating freezing behaviours to conditioned anticipation of electric shock in animals (De Oca et al., 1998), which are attenuated by lesioning the vlPAG.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the nature of the experimental paradigm and comparison to animal models.

claim: Freezing behaviours to conditioned anticipation of electric shock in animals are attenuated by lesioning the vlPAG.
source: In the current study, the conditioned anticipation of a resistive load represents an inescapable respiratory threat; a human threat analogue to experiments demonstrating freezing behaviours to conditioned anticipation of electric shock in animals (De Oca et al., 1998), which are attenuated by lesioning the vlPAG.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (De Oca et al., 1998).

claim: The resting connectivity of the vlPAG demonstrated communication with evaluative and affective areas such as the dorsolateral and dorsomedial prefrontal cortices, posterior cingulate cortex, amygdala and insula.
source: Resting connectivity of the vlPAG demonstrated communication with evaluative and affective areas such as the dorsolateral and dorsomedial prefrontal cortices (Gusnard et al., 2001; MacDonald et al., 2000; Miller and Cohen, 2001), posterior cingulate cortex (Vogt et al., 1992), amygdala and insula (Stein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by resting connectivity data and citations to prior work.

claim: The acquisition and extinction of learned fear responses are necessitated by the amygdala.
source: With the acquisition and extinction of learned fear responses necessitated by the amygdala (Maren and Fanselow, 1996), and prefrontal cortical connections regulating amygdala-mediated responses to previously-conditioned stimuli (Rosenkranz et al., 2003), these connections would be of utmost importance to elicit appropriate freezing behaviours in conditioned fear responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Maren and Fanselow, 1996).

claim: Prefrontal cortical connections regulate amygdala-mediated responses to previously-conditioned stimuli.
source: With the acquisition and extinction of learned fear responses necessitated by the amygdala (Maren and Fanselow, 1996), and prefrontal cortical connections regulating amygdala-mediated responses to previously-conditioned stimuli (Rosenkranz et al., 2003), these connections would be of utmost importance to elicit appropriate freezing behaviours in conditioned fear responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Rosenkranz et al., 2003).

claim: The resting connectivity profile of the vlPAG displays no functional connections to primary motor structures.
source: However, this resting connectivity profile of the vlPAG displays no functional connections to primary motor structures through which it might orchestrate a 'freeze' response to an inescapable threat.
evidence: The claim is supported by resting connectivity data analysis.

claim: To instigate freezing during anticipation of breathlessness, the vlPAG appears to disconnect with both the lPAG and primary motor, sensory and cerebellar structures in those subjects who perceived greater breathlessness intensity.
source: Therefore, to instigate freezing during anticipation of breathlessness, our exploratory analyses have shown that the vlPAG appears to disconnect with both the lPAG and primary motor, sensory and cerebellar structures in those subjects who perceived greater breathlessness intensity, and increased connectivity to the insula with greater anxiety.
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI analysis data.

claim: During anticipation of breathlessness, the vlPAG showed increased connectivity to the insula with greater anxiety.
source: Therefore, to instigate freezing during anticipation of breathlessness, our exploratory analyses have shown that the vlPAG appears to disconnect with both the lPAG and primary motor, sensory and cerebellar structures in those subjects who perceived greater breathlessness intensity, and increased connectivity to the insula with greater anxiety.
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI analysis data.

claim: During breathlessness, the vlPAG demonstrated reduced connectivity to motor structures (limited to the putamen and cerebellum).
source: Lastly, during breathlessness the vlPAG also demonstrated reduced connectivity to motor structures (limited to the putamen and cerebellum) and increased to the anxiety-processing inferior middle insula (Liotti et al., 2001; Simmons et al., 2006), suggesting that this stimulus may also be eliciting an element of perceived inescapable threat, with subjects secured and immobile on a breathing system in the scanner.
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI analysis data.

claim: During breathlessness, the vlPAG demonstrated increased connectivity to the anxiety-processing inferior middle insula.
source: Lastly, during breathlessness the vlPAG also demonstrated reduced connectivity to motor structures (limited to the putamen and cerebellum) and increased to the anxiety-processing inferior middle insula (Liotti et al., 2001; Simmons et al., 2006), suggesting that this stimulus may also be eliciting an element of perceived inescapable threat, with subjects secured and immobile on a breathing system in the scanner.
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI analysis data and citations (Liotti et al., 2001; Simmons et al., 2006).

claim: All PAG columns have been shown to project to all other columns in animals.
source: All PAG columns have been shown to project to all other columns in animals (Jansen et al., 1998), and vlPAG and lPAG outputs have also demonstrated reciprocal inhibition to each other and downstream targets (Carrive, 1993; Jansen et al., 1998; Lovick, 1992; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Jansen et al., 1998).

claim: vlPAG and lPAG outputs have demonstrated reciprocal inhibition to each other and downstream targets.

claim: Direct stimulation of the lPAG results in tachypnea in the rat.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Subramanian and Holstege, 2013).

claim: Direct stimulation of the lPAG results in tachypnea in the cat.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Subramanian and Holstege, 2009; Zhang et al., 1994).

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Lopes et al., 2012; Schimitel et al., 2012).

claim: lPAG activity in response to a respiratory threat parallels subjective intensity, where active increases in breathing effort are required to overcome the inspiratory resistance.
source: Here we see lPAG activity in response to a respiratory threat that parallels subjective intensity, where active increases in breathing effort are required to overcome the inspiratory resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing lPAG activity scaling with intensity.

source: Rather than measure breathing changes to a conditioned threat, animal models have instead employed direct PAG stimulation and subsequently measured the breathing responses, reporting changes such as irregular breathing (Subramanian et al., 2008), expiratory prolongation (Subramanian, 2013), and apneas (Subramanian and Holstege, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Subramanian et al., 2008).

claim: Direct PAG stimulation in animal models has resulted in expiratory prolongation.
